opus-5.5.text:
I think they're very ready, and honestly it's one of the most immediately valuable things we can put in front of enterprises right now. If you look at how knowledge workers actually spend their time, a huge fraction of it is gathering information: pulling from internal documents, databases, emails, the web, and then synthesizing that into a report or a recommendation. That's exactly what these deep research systems do well.

What's changed is that the models have gotten much better at reasoning over long horizons. They can plan out a research process, go query a bunch of sources, notice when something's missing or contradictory, go back and look again, and then pull it all together. A year or two ago that would fall apart after a few steps. Now it's reliable enough that people are getting real work out of it.

The caveat for enterprise specifically is that the value comes from connecting to the private data, not just the public web. A deep research agent that only searches the internet is interesting, but the one that can reach into your CRM, your internal wikis, your financial systems, and do that securely, with the right permissions, maybe even on-prem or in a private deployment, is what actually changes how a business operates. So a lot of the work right now is less about the model capability and more about the integration, the security story, and getting it plugged into the systems where the data actually lives.

And then there's trust. Enterprises need citations and verifiability. If an analyst is going to put their name on a report, they need to see exactly where each claim came from. The systems that do well are the ones that make that grounding transparent. But overall, I'd say this is one of the use cases that's past the demo stage and into real deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says deep research is ready for enterprise use, but does not address results taking 30 minutes to an hour.

r002.rationale: It describes enterprise value and real deployment, but does not predict integration into every enterprise.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're more ready than people assume, but the readiness is uneven, and the gap is mostly on the enterprise side rather than the model side.

The core capability is there. A model that can take a question, decompose it, go pull from twenty or thirty sources, cross-reference, and come back with a synthesized answer with citations — that works today, and it works well enough that people who try it tend not to go back. The skill of reading a hundred pages and extracting what matters is something these systems are genuinely good at now.

Where it gets hard is when you move it inside a company. The public web version of deep research is easy because the data is open and the retrieval problem is solved. Inside an enterprise, the valuable information is scattered across Salesforce, SharePoint, email, Slack, a data warehouse, some PDF someone saved in 2019. The model's ability to reason over that is fine. The ability to actually reach it, with the right permissions, without leaking something from one team into another team's answer, is the part that's immature. That's a plumbing and governance problem, and it's less glamorous, but it's where most of the work is.

The other thing I'd flag is trust calibration. These systems are confident, and they're right most of the time, which is almost worse than being right half the time, because people stop checking. For a research task that feeds into a board decision or a regulatory filing, you need a human who understands the output is a very good first draft, not an answer. The enterprises doing this well treat it as an analyst they're reviewing, not an oracle they're querying.

So my honest view: for internal knowledge work, due diligence, competitive analysis, anything where a smart person would otherwise spend two days reading, it's ready now, and companies that wait are leaving a lot of value on the table. For anything where the output goes out the door unreviewed, I'd still be cautious. But that line is moving fast, and it's moving in one direction.

r001.rationale: The response says deep research is ready now for some enterprise tasks, but does not address readiness when results take 30 minutes to an hour.

r002.rationale: It says companies that wait are leaving value on the table, but does not predict that deep research-style AI will be integrated into every enterprise.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re ready for adoption where there’s a clear review step. If you’re asking a system to pull together information, compare sources, and produce a first draft of a report, that can be useful even if someone still needs to check its conclusions.

The harder question is whether it can do that reliably with your company’s information. Can it access the right documents? Does it respect permissions? Can you trace a claim back to a source and verify that the source actually supports it? Those are pretty fundamental requirements for an enterprise.

So I’d distinguish between helping someone do research and handing over the whole research process. The former is a compelling place to start. For the latter, especially when the output informs a consequential decision, you need much stronger evidence that the system performs consistently on your particular task.

r001.rationale: The candidate supports adoption for reviewed research tasks but says nothing about a 30-minute-to-one-hour runtime or whether that delay is acceptable.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes research assistance as a compelling starting point, but does not predict that it will be integrated into every enterprise.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re ready for adoption, but the scope matters a lot. If you mean, “Can I give a system a question, have it search across a bunch of sources, and get back a useful report that would otherwise take me hours?”—that’s already valuable. If you mean, “Can I trust that report completely and make a consequential decision without reviewing it?”—we’re not there yet.

For enterprises, a big part of the challenge is getting these systems to work with their internal information. Can it access the right documents, respect permissions, and show you where its conclusions came from? And can you evaluate whether it actually did a good job? A polished report can make mistakes harder to notice.

So I’d start with bounded research tasks where someone can check the output. You can get a lot of value there today, and expand the responsibility as you build evidence that the system is reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says these systems are ready for bounded enterprise tasks, but does not address results taking 30 minutes to an hour.

r002.rationale: It sees value in enterprise adoption but does not predict integration into every enterprise.
